extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys/agents, and U.S. Patent and Trademark Office examiners handling international (PCT) and Hague design filings
extracted.subtask_description: Requirements, procedures, and legal effects for entering the U.S. national stage from an international (PCT) application and for filing/processing international design (Hague) applications designating the United States. Covers required documents, fees, deadlines, examination, publication, priority/benefit claims, and related criminal statutes and AIA provisions that affect patentability and post-grant remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: National stage: commencement and required submissions (35 U.S.C. 371(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon commencement of the national stage the applicant shall file in the Patent and Trademark Office: (1) the national fee provided in section 41(a); (2) a copy of the international application and an English translation if filed in another language (unless not required or already communicated); (3) amendments to the claims made under article 19 and translations if in another language (unless already communicated); (4) an oath or declaration of the inventor complying with section 115 and PTO regulations; and (5) an English translation of any annexes to the international preliminary examination report if in another language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These items are required by the date of commencement of the national stage unless the Director fixes a later time. Failure to comply is regarded as abandonment (or cancellation of Article 19 amendments). Director may require a surcharge to accept late national fee or oath/declaration. Applicant may present amendments to specification, claims and drawings after national stage commencement; applicant may request earlier commencement if the application is in order.

rubrics_metrics.name: National stage: commencement timing (35 U.S.C. 371(b),(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: The national stage commences with the expiration of the applicable time limit under treaty Articles (e.g., Article 22 or 39) subject to subsection (f). At the express request of the applicant, the national stage may be commenced at any time when the application is in order and subsection (c) requirements have been complied with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time limits under the treaty control default commencement; applicants may seek earlier commencement by express request, provided requirements are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: National stage: substantive and procedural determination (35 U.S.C. 372(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: All questions of substance and, within the scope of the treaty and Regulations, procedure in an international application designating the United States shall be determined as in the case of national applications regularly filed in the PTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTO applies national substantive law and applicable treaty/Regulation constraints when examining international (PCT) national-stage applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director powers for international applications (35 U.S.C. 372(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: For international applications designating but not originating in the U.S., the Director may reexamine form and content, may reexamine unity of invention under section 121 within treaty/Regulation scope, and may require verification of translations of the international application or related documents filed in a non-English language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner/Director may order additional reviews or translation verifications to ensure conformity with U.S. requirements and unity rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of international application (35 U.S.C. 374 & 374 (pre-AIA))
rubrics_metrics.description: The publication under the treaty of an international application designating the United States shall be deemed a publication under 35 U.S.C. 122(b) (and, pre-AIA, as provided in 35 U.S.C. 374 (pre-AIA)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treaty publication counts as U.S. publication for statutory purposes; check exceptions noted (e.g., section 154(d) or pre-AIA differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent issuance on an international application: effect and translation limitation (35 U.S.C. 375)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may issue a patent based on an international application designating the United States; such patent has the force and effect of a patent issued on a national application. If, due to an incorrect translation, the scope of a granted patent exceeds the scope of the international application in its original language, a court may retroactively limit the patent and declare unenforceable the extent the patent exceeds the original-language scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure accurate translations to avoid risk of later scope limitation or unenforceability; patents issued from PCT national stage are equivalent in force to national-filed patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees for international applications (35 U.S.C. 376 and related text)
rubrics_metrics.description: International and handling fees must be paid in U.S. currency. PTO shall charge a national fee under 41(a) and may also charge transmittal, search, supplemental search, preliminary examination, and other fees as specified in the Regulations. Amounts except international/handling fees are prescribed by the Director; Director may refund mistaken or excess payments and may refund parts of search, national, preliminary examination and additional fees where warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Regulations for fee amounts and payment timing. Director has authority to prescribe refunds and surcharges for late payments; certain surcharges may be imposed for later submission of fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions for Hague Agreement/Hague 'treaty' (35 U.S.C. 381(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Key definitions: 'treaty' = Geneva Act of the Hague Agreement (1999); 'regulations' capitalized = Common Regulations under the treaty, lowercase = Director's regulations under this title; 'designation' = request that an international registration have effect in a Contracting Party; 'International Bureau' = coordinating body under treaty/Regulations; 'effective registration date' = date of international registration determined by the International Bureau; 'international design application' = application for international registration; 'international registration' = international registration filed under the treaty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these statutory definitions when interpreting filing, priority, and procedural requirements for Hague international design filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility and filing procedure for international design applications (35 U.S.C. 382)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who is a U.S. national, or has domicile, habitual residence, or a real and effective industrial/commercial establishment in the U.S. may file an international design application by submitting an application and fees to the PTO as prescribed by the Director. PTO shall collect and transmit international fees to the International Bureau and forward international design applications to the International Bureau upon payment of a transmittal fee. Chapter 16 provisions apply except as otherwise provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check applicant eligibility under the statute, pay required transmittal fee, and comply with chapter 16 where applicable. International design application filed abroad or at the IB can count as a foreign filing under chapter 17 if filed in another country, at the IB, or with an intergovernmental organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required contents of an international design application (35 U.S.C. 383)
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to chapter 16 requirements, an international design application must contain: (1) a request for international registration under the treaty; (2) indication of designated Contracting Parties; (3) applicant data as prescribed; (4) copies of reproductions (or multiple reproductions) of the industrial design presented as prescribed; (5) an indication of the product(s) to which the design is applied as prescribed; (6) the fees prescribed; and (7) any other particulars prescribed in the Regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comply with treaty/Regulations for number/format of reproductions, product indications, and required data; missing or nonconforming items may affect filing/registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing date of international design application and Director review (35 U.S.C. 384)
rubrics_metrics.description: General rule: the filing date of an international design application in the U.S. is the effective registration date. An applicant may request Director review of the filing date; the Director may determine a different filing date and may establish procedures (including surcharge payment) to review filing date determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If filing date is critical for priority, use the Director review procedures and be prepared to pay any surcharge for review. Treat the effective registration date as the default filing date absent review/determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of international design application in the U.S. (35 U.S.C. 385)
rubrics_metrics.description: An international design application designating the United States shall have the effect, for all purposes from its filing date determined under section 384, of an application for patent filed in the PTO pursuant to chapter 16.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An international design application confers the same legal effect as a U.S. design application from the applicable filing date; use this when asserting priority or filing-date benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of priority and benefit claims for international design applications (35 U.S.C. 386)
rubrics_metrics.description: A national application is entitled to priority based on a prior international design application or prior foreign application consistent with conditions of sections 119/172. An international design application designating the U.S. may be entitled to priority based on prior foreign or prior international applications; benefit claims based on prior filings (including those that designated but did not originate in the U.S.) may require filing a certified copy and an English translation in the PTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming benefit of earlier filings, ensure compliance with statutory conditions and be prepared to submit certified copies/translations if the prior application did not originate in the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief from prescribed time limits for international design applications (35 U.S.C. 387)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to act within prescribed time limits may be excused upon a showing satisfactory to the Director of unintentional delay and under such conditions (including payment of the fee in section 41(a)(7)) as the Director may prescribe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely petitions for relief require showing unintentional delay and payment of prescribed fees; review Director's procedures for acceptable showings and required payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of withdrawal, renunciation, cancellation, or abandonment (35 U.S.C. 388)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an international design application designating the U.S. is withdrawn, renounced, canceled, or abandoned generally or as to the U.S. under treaty/Regulations, the U.S. designation has no effect after that date and is considered not made—unless a claim for benefit of an earlier filing date was made before the withdrawal. Withdrawn/abandoned international applications may still serve as a basis for priority under sections 386 or 365 if they designated a country other than the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make benefit/priority claims before withdrawal dates to preserve rights; withdrawn international filings may still provide priority under certain circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination and issuance for international design applications (35 U.S.C. 389)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director shall cause an examination of an international design application designating the U.S. pursuant to this title. All questions of substance and, unless required otherwise by treaty/Regulations, procedures shall be determined as for chapter 16 applications. The Director may prescribe fees for filing, designating the U.S., and other processing and may provide for later payment of such fees (including surcharges). The Director may issue a patent based on an international design application, with the same force and effect as a chapter 16 application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International design applications undergo substantive U.S. examination; follow PTO fee/payment rules and treaty constraints in prosecution and issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of international design applications (35 U.S.C. 390)
rubrics_metrics.description: The publication under the treaty of an international design application designating the U.S. shall be deemed a publication under 35 U.S.C. 122(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treaty publication triggers the same statutory publication consequences as U.S. publication under section 122(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: False statements and criminal penalties applicable to patent proceedings (18 U.S.C. 1001)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever, in any matter within the jurisdiction of the executive, legislative, or judicial branch, knowingly and willfully falsifies, conceals, or covers up a material fact, makes materially false statements, or makes/uses false writings or documents containing materially false statements, shall be fined or imprisoned (up to 5 years, or more in certain contexts). Subsection (b) carves out certain judicial proceeding submissions. Subsection (c) limits legislative-branch application to administrative matters and investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oaths, declarations, submissions to the PTO, and other filings are subject to 18 U.S.C. 1001; applicants and practitioners must ensure truthfulness in all filings to avoid criminal exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment or destruction of public records (18 U.S.C. 2071)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever willfully and unlawfully conceals, removes, mutilates, obliterates, destroys, or attempts to do so, any record, proceeding, map, book, paper, or other thing filed with any court or public office, shall be fined or imprisoned (up to three years), and persons in custody of such records who willfully do so may forfeit their office and be disqualified from holding any United States office (with limited exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improper handling or destruction of patent office records or related documents can give rise to criminal penalties; maintain custody and integrity of files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax strategies deemed within the prior art (AIA §14)
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of evaluating an invention under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103, any strategy for reducing, avoiding, or deferring tax liability shall be deemed insufficient to differentiate a claimed invention from the prior art. Exclusions apply for inventions used solely for preparing tax returns or purely financial-management technology to the extent severable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims directed to tax strategies are treated as lacking novelty/obviousness distinction from prior art; craft claims to recite patent-eligible technological improvements or fall into statutory exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional program for covered business method patents (AIA §18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishes a transitional post-grant review proceeding for covered business method (CBM) patents, to be implemented by Director regulations and employing post-grant review standards/procedures with specified exceptions and limitations (e.g., who may petition, prior-art limitations). Defines CBM patents as those claiming methods/apparatus for data processing or operations used in financial product/service practice, administration, or management, excluding patents for technological inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CBM review has special standing and scope rules (e.g., petitioner requirement related to being sued), venue/appeal/stay considerations for civil litigation apply, and Director must issue regs to determine 'technological invention' status. Use caution when asserting/defending CBM patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay factors for civil actions in relation to transitional proceedings (AIA §18(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When a party seeks a stay of civil infringement litigation pending a transitional proceeding, the court shall consider whether a stay will simplify issues and streamline trial; whether discovery is complete and a trial date set; whether a stay (or denial) would unduly prejudice the nonmoving party or present tactical advantage; and whether stay/denial will reduce litigation burden on parties/court. Immediate interlocutory appeal to the Federal Circuit is permitted; Federal Circuit reviews district court's decision for consistent application of precedent and may review de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts balance case management and prejudice concerns when considering stays related to CBM/post-grant proceedings; expect appellate review for consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on issuing patents directed to human organisms (AIA §33)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding any other law, no patent may issue on a claim directed to or encompassing a human organism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure claims do not attempt to claim human organisms; such claims are statutorily forbidden.
